papers.title: Finite element analysis of different subtrochanteric osteotomy techniques in total hip arthroplasty for high hip dislocation
papers.abstract: Aims Subtrochanteric shortening osteotomy in total hip arthroplasty (THA) for developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) has variable outcomes. This study evaluated the initial stability of seven different osteotomy techniques. Methods A 3D finite element model of a femur with a stem was created. Seven models simulating osteotomies with different angles (0°, 45°, 90°, -90°, 120°, -120°, z-shaped) were analyzed. Outcomes included range of motion (ROM), bone/implant stress, and osteotomy surface separation. Results The 0° model had the greatest ROM (lowest stiffness). The z-shaped and -90° designs provided the best rotational stability. Analysis of the centre of rotation showed single-symmetric models (45°, z-shaped) shifted laterally, suggesting a ‘windshield wiper’ effect, while double-symmetric models (90°, -90°, 120°, -120°) stayed aligned with the prosthesis axis. Stress patterns differed: single-symmetric models concentrated stress on the lesser trochanter, while double-symmetric models stressed the greater trochanter, with a notable ring in the -90° design. Implant stresses were similar, except in the horizontal model. The -90° and 90° models had the least osteotomy separation, unlike the 45° model. Conclusion No single osteotomy technique outperformed others in all metrics. The z-shaped and -90° designs offered the best rotational stability; the -90° and 90° designs minimized axial separation; the 45° model showed the worst ‘windshield wiper’ effect. The 120° technique provided a balanced profile with moderate rotational stability, acceptable separation, and less pronounced stress rings, representing a reasonable compromise. The choice should be guided by clinical priorities. Cite this article: Bone Joint Res 2026;15(11):1364–1373.

papers.title: K/Ce/Sm multiple-doped CaBi 2 Nb 2 O 9 aurivillius-type ceramics used for high-temperature piezoelectric ultrasonic transducer
papers.abstract: Abstract Aurivillius-type CaBi2Nb2O9 (CBN) is attractive for high-temperature ultrasonic sensing owing to its high Curie temperature (TC ≈ 940 ℃). However, its weak piezoelectric response and loss of polarization alignment during thermal exposure limit its practical performance. Herein, K/Ce/Sm co-substitution at the Ca site was employed to modify the lattice structure, electrical transport, and domain morphology of CBN ceramics. Co-substitution reduced the orthorhombic distortion while preserving the orthorhombic framework. The optimized CBN-KCS-12 ceramic exhibited a piezoelectric coefficient d33 of 18 pC/N, a TC of approximately 933 ℃, and a ρdc resistivity of 2.59 × 106 Ω·cm at 650 ℃, approximately 18.5 times that of undoped CBN. The annealing temperature corresponding to 50% retention of the initial d₃₃ increased from 600 to 850 ℃, and CBN-KCS-12 retained approximately 44% of its initial d33 after annealing at 900 ℃. Piezoresponse force microscopy revealed larger block-like regions in CBN-KCS-12 compared with the fine stripe-like patterns in undoped CBN, with block-like contrast also observed after annealing at 900 ℃. The elastic modulus also increased from 30.1 to 33.8 GPa. Finally, a single-element ultrasonic transducer fabricated from CBN-KCS-12 produced clear pulse-echo signals from room temperature to 400 ℃, achieving a signal-to-noise ratio above 36 dB and a -6 dB fractional bandwidth of approximately 42% at 400 °C. These results demonstrate the potential of multi-element A-site co-substitution for improving CBN ceramics for high-temperature ultrasonic applications.

papers.title: Aprendizagem significativa e crítica no ensino de matemática: uma prática pedagógica com base na escala de proficiência do SAEB
papers.abstract: This experience report presents a pedagogical practice conducted with students aged 11–12 years to foster meaningful learning in mathematics, focusing on the concept of area. The proposal was grounded in the Theory of Critical Meaningful Learning and employed active learning methodologies that encouraged participation, inquiry, and reflection. The teaching strategy was informed by the proficiency scale of Brazil’s National Basic Education Assessment System (SAEB), aligning classroom activities with the competencies assessed. The results indicate that integrating data from large-scale educational assessments with contextualized teaching practices improved students’ performance and strengthened meaningful learning. The findings suggest that combining educational theory with classroom practice and using assessment indicators to guide instruction can enhance Mathematics teaching and foster critical and meaningful learning.

papers.title: The cost of enforcing long-run coverage: a phase transition in online conformal prediction
papers.abstract: Consider an online prediction setting, where at each time, we are given a new feature vector and asked to provide a prediction interval or prediction set that will likely contain the corresponding response. In this setting, if the data points are i.i.d. (or more generally, exchangeable), conformal prediction provides a mechanism for building valid prediction sets around the output of any trained model, offering coverage probability $\geq 1-α$ at each time $t$. In practice, however, issues such as distribution drift, changepoints, or other challenges may cause violations of the i.i.d. assumption. In this adversarial setting, online conformal prediction methods can still offer guarantees on long-run empirical coverage. However, there is a trade-off between these two types of goals: enforcing tight constraints on long-run empirical coverage to protect against the adversarial setting can lead to unstable oscillations in the instantaneous training-conditional coverage in the i.i.d. setting.   In this work, we seek best-of-both-worlds algorithms that aim to minimize cumulative error in instantaneous training-conditional coverage when in the i.i.d. setting, while also offering long-run empirical coverage guarantees in the adversarial setting. Specifically, consider a condition that requires long-run empirical coverage to deviate from the target level $1-α$ by at most $\mathcal{O}(T^{-β})$, for some $β\in[0,1]$. We prove that this family of conditions can be described with a phase transition. For $β\in[0,\frac{1}{2}]$, it is possible to construct algorithms satisfying such a constraint in the adversarial setting, while offering the same instantaneous coverage performance as split conformal prediction if the data is in fact i.i.d. On the other hand, for $β\in(\frac{1}{2},1]$, this type of condition comes at a cost, and does not achieve best-of-both-worlds behavior.

papers.title: Lazy-MOSAIC: Accelerating Skill-Centric Manipulation Planning with Learned Skill-Effect World Models
papers.abstract: Long-horizon manipulation tasks require a robot to perform a sequence of physical interactions with its environment, typically combining several different skills. Planning such behaviors efficiently is challenging: given a library of parameterized skills, solutions lie in a vast hybrid space of skill sequences and their parameters, and evaluating each candidate skill's feasibility and effect with a high-fidelity world model such as a physics simulator is computationally expensive. MOSAIC, a recent skill-centric approach, lets the skills guide a non-sequential search toward the regions of this space where they are likely to succeed; however, it pays the full cost of simulation for every parameterized skill it considers. In this work, we introduce Lazy-MOSAIC, a lazy planning framework that instead searches over hypothesized skill outcomes. A cheap learned skill-effect world model predicts, in a fraction of a millisecond, a skill's feasibility and the world state it produces. Lazy-MOSAIC then uses these predictions to focus expensive simulation on promising candidate skills and, when a hypothesis is invalidated, repairs only the affected part of the search, while ensuring that every skill in a returned plan is validated in simulation. We evaluate Lazy-MOSAIC on cluttered-shelf retrieval tasks of increasing difficulty and demonstrate it on a physical robot, showing that it plans substantially faster than baselines with fewer simulator queries, while matching or exceeding their success rate in every setting. Visit skill-mosaic.github.io.

papers.title: LynnReal-Hand: Unlocking World Interaction with Hand Control
papers.abstract: Interactive video world models enable exploration through text and camera controls, yet direct object interaction requires finer control. Hands provide a natural interface, but translating continuous hand movements into coherent visual responses remains challenging because of complex hand-object dynamics and demanding real-time computation. To address these challenges, we introduce LynnReal-Hand, a hand-controlled video world model that unifies precise interaction modeling with efficient streaming generation. We curate 100K interaction clips spanning diverse real and synthetic environments and develop hand-aware supervision to improve fine-grained hand motions and object interactions. Building on this foundation, we learn a causal flow map for few-step generation and introduce region-aware score distillation that combines complementary video and image priors to refine interaction dynamics and visual appearance. To further reduce inference latency, we propose Ultra-Fast-VAE, a compact video decoder that preserves high reconstruction fidelity with substantially lower computational cost. Extensive evaluations on HandBench demonstrate superior hand-following accuracy and visual quality compared with existing approaches. Our full-sequence model achieves an FVD of 181.67 and a MANO Dice score of 93.02, while the three-step causal model maintains a MANO Dice score of 92.49. For real-time interaction, 540p streaming on a single H200 reaches 18.03 FPS with 741ms latency and an optimized peak GPU memory footprint of only 34.89GB. We will release the datasets, model weights, and the full training and inference code to support research on hand-controlled video world models.

papers.title: Variationally correct physics-informed operator learning for nonlinear partial differential equations
papers.abstract: Physics-informed operator learning trains neural operators on the residual of a parametric partial differential equation (PDE) instead of labeled solution data, but its reliability depends on a variationally correct residual: one that is equivalent to the error in a norm dictated by the equation, the PDE-compliant norm. For nonlinear equations written as first-order systems, we prove that the first-order system least-squares residual is equivalent to the error in this norm near a solution branch if the linearized residual is stable and the residual derivative is Lipschitz continuous, possibly in a norm stronger than the error norm. We verify these conditions for monotone reaction, solution- and gradient-dependent diffusion, and compressible Neo-Hookean hyperelasticity. The stability mechanisms vary across these classes, as do the regions where the equivalence holds, from arbitrary bounded sets to a neighborhood of the branch. In a conforming finite element space, we show that the loss excess of a state near the finite element solution is equivalent to its squared distance from that solution. We use this loss to train a reduced basis neural operator with values in this space, with solution snapshots needed only for the basis and the loss and its symbolically derived gradient assembled by the finite element library. At inference, this loss estimates the error. Numerically, the square root of the loss excess tracks the error within factors comparable to those of the linear case, and the operator achieves higher accuracy in the PDE-compliant norm than grid-based baselines evaluated in the same finite element space.

papers.title: Warm Starting Neural Dynamics Models From Few Jacobian Samples
papers.abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) leverages a model of the environment, used for planning and generating samples without interacting with the real world. Motivated by evidence that informed initialization significantly improves the efficiency of MBRL, we propose TDec-Init, an algorithm to warm-start neural dynamics models using transition Jacobians. Using a decoupling algorithm based on the decomposition of a tensor of stacked Jacobian samples, we recover weights and flexible nonlinearities, and use them to initialize a feedforward neural network. In the low-data regime, we show on several benchmark environments that our approach outperforms random initialization and value training, and either matches or outperforms Sobolev training, while requiring fewer training steps between episodes.

papers.title: Efficient Modeling of Multi-Agent Systems via Structure-Aware Physics-Informed Learning
papers.abstract: Modeling large multi-agent systems poses challenges for trajectory inference and parameter identification, as network size and coupling increase computational demands and partial observations require reconstructing unobserved states. We propose MAS-PINN, a neural-network architecture with a tailored training algorithm for a physics-informed learning framework that leverages the network topology and the agents' similarity to reduce computational and memory costs of simulating and identifying multi-agent systems. Its architecture represents agent trajectories through shared temporal features and agent-specific coefficients. Training alternates between learning features, fitting coupled trajectories, and estimating physical parameters. A matrix-free update exploits local interactions to fit trajectories without forming large global matrices. Experiments on Lorenz rings, Lotka--Volterra networks, and Rössler oscillators show improved trajectory and parameter accuracy over baselines, including inference in large systems and identification under partial observations or unknown topology, alongside substantial computational savings in coefficient fitting.

papers.title: Data-Driven Predictive Control for Autonomous Vehicle Racing under Varying Friction
papers.abstract: Data-driven predictive control (DPC) predicts future outputs by combining recorded input-output trajectory data such that the combined trajectory approximately matches a measured initial trajectory and tracks a provided reference. This paper investigates to what extent and under which conditions DPC using data pooled across operating conditions retains the prediction accuracy of DPC using data from the current operating condition. In autonomous vehicle racing, the tire-road friction varies between racetrack sections and tire sets. If the initial trajectory and the recorded data originate from different frictions, prediction accuracy of DPC degrades. Ensuring the frictions match requires knowing the friction during recording and estimating the current friction explicitly. Instead, we pool data recorded at different frictions. We compare the prediction accuracy of DPC using data recorded under the current friction (matched), a different friction (mismatched) and data pooled from both frictions. We evaluate in simulation and small-scale vehicle experiments in the Cyber-Physical Mobility Lab (CPM Lab). Our results show that pooled data keep the multi-step root-mean-square prediction error within 1.5 times that of matched data, whereas mismatched data increase it by a factor of 2.2 to 3.4. To assess how this prediction accuracy carries over to control, we evaluate the tracking error from the raceline in closed loop. In simulation, DPC with pooled data tracks comparably to nonlinear model predictive control (13.7 cm versus 13.3 cm) and close to DPC with matched data in the CPM Lab, differing by 0.1 cm on the low-friction tires (1.6 cm versus 1.5 cm) and by 0.2 cm on the high-friction tires (0.9 cm versus 1.1 cm). DPC thus provides partial adaptation to varying friction, without a dedicated adaptation method.

papers.title: Certified Nash Equilibrium Learning for Nonzero-Sum Jump-Diffusion Games: Policy Iteration and Off-Policy Q-Learning
papers.abstract: This paper establishes two model-free reinforcement learning methods for infinite-horizon N-player linear-quadratic nonzero-sum stochastic differential games whose drift, Brownian diffusion, and Poisson jump amplitudes depend on all players' controls. Control dependence in the diffusion and jump terms couples the players' simultaneous feedback updates. A verifiable certificate ensures that the partially model-free policy iteration map is contractive on an invariant closed ball centered at an admissible initial feedback profile. All feedback iterates are mean-square stabilizing, and the algorithm achieves local geometric convergence of feedback gains and value matrices to those associated with a closed-loop Nash equilibrium. The term certified refers to a verifiable convergence certificate that guarantees mean-square stability of all policy iterates and local geometric convergence to a closed-loop Nash equilibrium. To implement the policy updates from data, the off-policy Q-learning algorithm reuses the same behavior-policy data across iterations without requiring the system coefficients or jump intensity. Under quantitative persistence of excitation and a common initialization, exact population regression reproduces the policy-iteration sequence. The same local convergence guarantee therefore applies to off-policy Q-learning at the population level. Simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of the two proposed algorithms.

papers.title: QuantileGS: Quantile-Based Conformal Bounds on RGB Rendering Errors for Novel View Synthesis with 3D Gaussian Splatting
papers.abstract: Uncertainty quantification for novel view synthesis with 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) assesses rendering reliability at unseen viewpoints. This reliability depends on the discrepancy between rendered and true colors, which cannot be measured without ground-truth images. We therefore quantify uncertainty in this unknown discrepancy through upper bounds on per-pixel RGB mean absolute error. However, learned bounds may underestimate these errors and overstate rendering reliability, motivating calibration to a prescribed coverage level. In this paper, we propose QuantileGS, a post-hoc framework that combines learned rendering-error quantiles with scale-normalized conformal calibration to produce spatially adaptive error bounds. The framework comprises three phases. Phase 1, Rendering-Error Computation, measures RGB mean absolute error between observed images and predictions from a frozen 3DGS model. Phase 2, Ordered Gaussian Quantile Fields, learns two scalar attributes per Gaussian to predict lower and upper rendering-error quantiles. Phase 3, Scale-Normalized Conformal Calibration, calibrates the upper prediction on held-out images, using the quantile gap to scale the correction. Under the stated assumptions, the resulting bounds provide finite-sample marginal coverage. At a nominal coverage level of 90%, calibration raises mean empirical test coverage from 69.6% to 89.6% on LLFF and from 80.1% to 92.1% on Mip-NeRF 360. On LF, coverage remains conservative at 96.3% before and 96.4% after calibration. Applications to active view selection, Gaussian pruning, and RGB-D simultaneous localization and mapping illustrate how these bounds inform downstream decisions.

papers.title: Heteroscedastic Gaussian Process Q-learning for Sample Efficient Experimentation
papers.abstract: Self-driving laboratories must learn to control a process from tens to hundreds of expensive experiments, too few for deep reinforcement learning (RL). We learn the Q-function directly with a Gaussian process (GP), which avoids learning the dynamics, and show that the GP posterior supplies the learning rate of Q-learning. If each Bellman target is treated as a noisy measurement of the Q-function, the learning rate that minimises the mean squared error is the Kalman gain, and applying it to every observed transition is equivalent to GP regression. Heteroscedastic Gaussian Process Q-learning (HGPQ) sets the noise variance of each target with a heteroscedastic GP, which learns how unreliable the targets are across the states and inputs. Targets from noisy operating conditions, or from regions where the value function has large gradients, then move the estimate less than targets from low-noise regions, so HGPQ learns quickly where the data are reliable without being misled where they are not. For kernel value iteration with per-target variances that are assigned when a target is collected, we prove a high-probability bound on the error of the value estimate, uniform over the explored region. Pooled over five simulated benchmarks, which include a chemical reactor and a bioprocess, HGPQ approaches the best return found by any method in fewer episodes than GP, kernel and deep RL baselines.

papers.title: BoBDeLaN: Bounded-Bandwidth Context Adaptation for Deep Lagrangian Robot Control
papers.abstract: Learned physics-based models provide structure for robot control, but uncertain payloads and unmodeled dynamics limit their predictive accuracy. Context-aware Deep Lagrangian Networks enable adaptation through a latent context inferred from measurement histories while retaining Lagrangian structure for each fixed context. However, this structure alone does not constrain sensitivity to measurement disturbances. We introduce BoBDeLaN, which combines a contracting, gain-bounded Recurrent Equilibrium Network context encoder with stable linear filtering to shape disturbance sensitivity across frequencies. This architecture guarantees exponential forgetting of the recurrent initialization and admits a finite-horizon, frequency-weighted bound on context perturbations, which extends to residual torque prediction under a Lipschitz continuity assumption on the context-conditioned dynamics model. We evaluate a low-pass realization within model predictive control on simulated and real hardware manipulation tasks, together with frequency-sensitivity analysis on real-robot data. Compared with an LSTM encoder using the same input filter, BoBDeLaN exhibits reduced high-frequency context sensitivity, lower residual torque prediction error, and smoother motion, with less degradation under injected disturbances.

papers.title: Polygraph: Large-Scale Multi-Session Trajectory Optimization using Pose Graphs
papers.abstract: Robots, vehicles, and wearable devices often traverse the same environment many times. Each pass produces its own trajectory from onboard visual or visual-inertial odometry. These trajectories are locally accurate but drift over time and live in unrelated coordinate frames. Turning many such independent trajectories into one globally consistent set is the large-scale multi-session trajectory optimization problem. Existing solutions largely work offline. All sessions must be available up front, one session is fixed as the reference frame, and a single fused map is then optimized. This paper presents Polygraph, a multi-session trajectory optimization pipeline that processes sessions online, one keyframe and one spatial cluster at a time, and never builds a 3D map. Keyframes are grouped into local clusters. When a cluster closes, it is matched against every other session through learned image retrieval. Candidate pairs are verified with sparse feature matching, monocular metric depth, and robust pose estimation. A two-tier consensus gate admits a cross-session edge into the shared pose graph only once independent evidence corroborates it. A cheap incremental solve keeps the graph current, and a periodic robust batch solve prunes outliers. We evaluate Polygraph on stereo outdoor driving, HoloLens and iPad indoor traversals, legged indoor locomotion with a Boston Dynamics Spot, and large-scale outdoor vehicle and handheld routes. Against the closest prior work on the same GPU model, using its reported timings, Polygraph runs faster, commits fewer loop-closure edges, and matches or improves on accuracy.

papers.title: Comfort as a Constraint or as a Cost in Reinforcement Learning and Model Predictive Building Control
papers.abstract: A building controller that keeps a zone within comfort bounds at minimum energy can treat the bounds as a soft constraint, by adding the weighted violation to its cost, or as a hard constraint. We analyze the effect of the hard and the soft formulation of the same problem and isolate the effect of the formulation from the effect of the algorithm. To this end, we measure the difference in energy use between the two formulations on the BOPTEST bestest_hydronic_heat_pump case, in model predictive control (MPC) and in reinforcement learning (RL). The soft formulations are a weighted MPC and weighted SAC and DDPG learners, each at twelve weights. The hard formulations are an MPC with an exact penalty and the Lagrangian learners SAC-Lagrangian and primal-dual DDPG. We find that the hard formulations use more energy than the soft formulations at the largest weight, but violate the comfort bounds less. For a large weight, the soft formulation approaches the behavior of the hard formulation. The frontiers of the energy-comfort trade-off of the three weighted controllers lie close to each other, and the weight selects an operating point on this frontier. Under the soft formulation, the three algorithms reach very similar operating points, although at somewhat different weights. For this HVAC problem, the formulation and the weight thus affect the energy use more than the choice of algorithm.

papers.title: Driving the Style: Velocity-Conditioned Whole-Body Control from Motion Demonstrations
papers.abstract: Achieving human-like behavior on humanoid robots has advanced rapidly by leveraging motion-capture demonstrations rather than hand-crafted cost functions. Adversarial imitation supplies a style signal that lets a policy fulfill a task while adhering to a desired style, but is difficult to transfer to hardware. Whole-body tracking through reinforcement learning instead deploys reliably and imitates demonstrations faithfully, but the resulting policies are conditioned on the future reference, so they require a reference trajectory at runtime and can fail when the motion differs from the training data. We train a humanoid policy directly with whole-body tracking rewards while restricting its actor to compact locomotion commands and robot observations. Reference motion supervises the reward and privileged critic, without supplying reference joint trajectories to the actor or requiring teacher distillation. The demonstrated style is thereby encoded in the policy through the tracking reward, so the robot reproduces the whole-body style under commanded velocities. Trained on a single random-walk motion and commanded with velocity profiles from held-out motions, our policy reaches at least 98\% success in simulation and completes every trial on the Unitree G1. On held-out slow walking, whole-body tracking drops to 2\% success and command-conditioned distillation to 56\%, and both fail on the real robot. On the trained motions, the joint position error of our policy stays within 8\% of whole-body tracking, and it has a higher style coverage than adversarial motion priors (AMP), which fell on the real robot without a safety crane.

papers.title: artist: A Python package for differentiable ray tracing and gradient-based optimization of solar tower power plant operation
papers.abstract: Solar tower power plants provide dispatchable, renewable energy by concentrating sunlight with thousands of mirrors, called heliostats, onto a central receiver. Efficient operation requires accurate modeling of the optical path from each heliostat to the receiver and compensation for manufacturing imperfections, kinematic misalignment, and material degradation that distort the flux distribution. Conventional ray tracers predict the flux from an assumed plant model but are limited to forward simulation. They cannot recover unknown plant parameters from measured flux nor directly optimize plant operation. We present artist, an open-source, FAIR4RS-compliant Python package implementing a fully differentiable digital twin of solar tower power plants. By making the optical pipeline, comprising heliostat surface representation, kinematics, blocking, and ray tracing, end to end differentiable, artist turns the digital twin from a passive forward model into an active physics-based tool for inverse modeling and data-driven optimization. The resulting gradient-based framework unifies tasks usually handled by separate solutions, such as reconstructing heliostat surfaces and kinematics from operational flux images without costly deflectometry, predicting irradiance at the receiver, and optimizing aim points to realize a desired receiver flux density distribution. Built on PyTorch, artist scales to real plants through GPU acceleration, a structure-of-arrays memory layout, and nested data parallelism. It interfaces with open data sources such as the PAINT database. We describe the software architecture, physical models, and optimization framework, and demonstrate the workflow on representative tasks. By integrating modeling, prediction, and optimization into a single open, interpretable package, artist provides a principled foundation for data-driven research toward autonomous solar tower operation.

papers.title: Auditing World-Model Explanations in Retail Forecasting: Faithfulness, Accuracy and Price Response
papers.abstract: Forecasting models that read the price and promotion plan explain each forecast as a baseline, what would sell with nothing planned, plus the lift the plan adds. We test such explanations with eight checks, six with a pass rule fixed before any result, and find that passing them does not make an explanation right. In generated store data with known effects, a world model passes the checks of construction, stability, price direction and agreement with sales and with LightGBM, yet its lifts are 1.33 to 1.40 times the truth when merchants plan into high-demand weeks, and 1.23 to 1.42 times in eight variants of that world. It still picks the right weeks to promote, but stock ordered to its lift is off by 0.44 to 0.48 of the true lift. Its stated response to a lasting regular-price change is 4.7 to 6.5 times the true -0.5, and only a measured cause finds this. On Dominick's, 38 episodes in which a store's regular prices sat apart from its zone peers give a noisy benchmark: a pooled 8-week response of -0.33 (95% interval -0.68 to 0.01). For the final tuned world models of our companion paper on nine data sets, baseline and lift add up under each model's own plan, but a deeper price cut lowers the forecast in 29% to 83% of item-week steps on Dominick's (23% to 80% within prices seen in training), and the world model and LightGBM both state about twice the measured response. Across 703 configurations from the settings searches, checks passed were not related to forecast accuracy (Spearman 0.02, 95% interval -0.02 to 0.05); with no known answer for those versions, this concerns accuracy, while whether an explanation is right is measured only in the generated data.

papers.title: QTOP: Scaling Humanoid Motion Tracking with Quantile Critics
papers.abstract: Learning human motion tracking policies through reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a core capability that underpins a majority of recent progress in humanoid whole-body control. However, achieving generalization to unseen motions at high fidelity requires jointly scaling training to thousands of GPU and dataset hours. This work hypothesizes that motion tracking is inherently compute-bound because training on a diverse set of motions introduces learning interference, similar to multi-task RL. To tackle this, we propose Quantile Tracking Optimization (QTOP), which improves sample efficiency by introducing a distributional advantage estimate conditioned on state and reference pairs. QTOP outperforms on and off-policy RL baselines both in simulation and real-world tracking scenarios on multiple datasets by up to 10\%. Furthermore, we establish a scaling law for QTOP and find that, aside from scaling predictably, dataset size has minimal impact on performance for moderately sized GPU hour regimes.

papers.title: Newton-PINet: A fast physics-informed neural network with Newton linearization for meta-learning nonlinear PDEs
papers.abstract: Scientific machine learning has opened new avenues for solving parameterized partial differential equations (PDEs), enabling models to learn a family of PDEs and generalize to unseen instances. In this context, data-driven operator learning methods typically require large training datasets, while physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) suffer from difficult optimization and limited generalization, especially for nonlinear PDEs. We propose Newton-PINet, a physics-informed network enhanced by Newton linearization, offering an effective meta-learning framework for nonlinear PDEs. Newton-PINet (i) employs a physics-informed multilayer network with skip connections, where the output-layer weights are solved by least squares; (ii) adopts a two-stage learning strategy that first leverages gradient-based training to learn robust representations from the available training tasks, and then performs gradient-free fine-tuning on the output layer for fast task-specific generalization; and (iii) incorporates a Newton linearization method to speed up the least-squares iteration for nonlinear PDE problems. On a challenging nonlinear reaction-diffusion benchmark, Newton-PINet achieves up to three orders of magnitude lower relative error than recent neural solvers, while using 16x fewer training tasks and over an order of magnitude less training time (about 5 minutes versus several hours). This work advances the meta-learning of PINNs toward data-efficient, fast, and generalizable physics solvers. The code and datasets are publicly available at: https://github.com/fycAIwj/Newton-PINet.

papers.title: DNA: A Double-Helix Hierarchical Deep Interaction Network Architecture for Industrial Digital Twin
papers.abstract: High-fidelity modeling is fundamental to industrial digital twin, yet a trade-off persists between the physical transparency of mechanistic models and the superior predictive power of data-driven approaches. Existing hybrid methods often fail to bridge this gap, suffering from shallow integration and rigid one-shot modeling strategies that struggle with complex industrial systems. To address these issues, we propose a \textbf{Double-Helix Hierarchical Deep Interaction Network Architecture (DNA)}. Inspired by the double-helix structure of biological \textit{DNA}, our architecture intertwines mechanistic and data-driven modeling strands through two novel interaction strategies, forming a symbiotic architecture in which the two strands mutually enhance predictive capability. Furthermore, the hierarchical structure of DNA allows it to model complex systems in a multi-stage manner through two tailored deep learning frameworks. We evaluate the proposed approach on two distinct industrial systems, where DNA achieves reductions in MAE of 3.704\% and 3.175\%, respectively, compared to the strongest baseline. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of DNA and suggest its potential to provide new insights for the development of industrial digital twins.

papers.title: Neural Operator Approximation for Yau--Yau Nonlinear Filtering: Stability, Approximation, and Fast Computation
papers.abstract: Since the introduction of the Kalman filter, nonlinear state estimation has become an important topic in areas such as aerospace engineering, sensor design, and target tracking. Within the optimal filtering framework described by the Duncan-Mortensen-Zakai (DMZ) equation, Yau-Yau filtering (YYF) employs an offline-online decomposition: the Fokker-Planck-Kolmogorov (FKE) equations, initialized by a prescribed set of basis functions, are solved offline, and the prior density is projected onto these basis functions during the online stage. However, this approach still faces two computational challenges: solving multiple FKEs offline can be computationally expensive, and the online projection becomes costly when filtering is performed repeatedly or in high-dimensional settings. To address these limitations, we develop a neural operator filter (NOF) that directly learns the mapping from the prior density to the posterior density, thereby eliminating both the expensive offline FKE solves and the online projection. The underlying operator is approximated using a Fourier neural operator (FNO). Numerical experiments on several challenging filtering systems verify both the effectiveness and accuracy of our method, and we further provide a rigorous theoretical analysis of its stability and approximation error.

papers.title: JEPTERA: A Platform Agnostic JEPA-Assisted Model Predictive Planner for Urban UAV Navigation
papers.abstract: Urban navigation for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) requires planning that accounts for environmental geometry, vehicle dynamics, and moving obstacles. This paper presents JEPTERA, a navigation architecture that integrates a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA), Model Predictive Control (MPC), PID control, and a safety layer. JEPA predicts the UAV's motion response to candidate commands for MPC action selection, while the safety layer checks trajectories against occupied space and predicted obstacle motion. Simulator adapters and platform-specific YAML configurations separate the planning core from simulator interfaces. An ablation study evaluated six configurations across three gym scenarios, totaling 180 runs. The complete architecture achieved the highest aggregate success rate, completing 28 of 30 runs. Additional tests completed one route across three city maps without collisions. Separate integration tests demonstrated operation in Gazebo/ROS 2, MuJoCo, and CARLA without modifying the core planning logic. These results support the feasibility of the integrated architecture for simulated urban UAV navigation and its portability across simulator interfaces.

papers.title: A bound-preserving hybrid lattice Boltzmann method for scalar hyperbolic conservation laws
papers.abstract: Solutions to scalar hyperbolic conservation laws may develop discontinuities within finite time even from smooth initial data, while higher-order lattice Boltzmann (LB) methods tend to generate non-physical oscillations and out-of-bounds behavior near steep gradients. To address this issue, we first construct a first-order LB method with the upwind-type equilibrium distribution functions under the \(DdQ(2d+1)\) lattice structure, and establish its bound-preserving (BP) conditions. We then develop a second-order multiple-relaxation-time LB (MRT-LB) method by introducing the auxiliary source distribution functions, and analyze its \(L^2\) stability. Building on these, we propose a hybrid LB method that preserves the collision-streaming structure, by conservatively mixing first- and second-order updates through a convex constraint mechanism. We further establish the global BP (GBP), local BP (LBP), and relaxed LBP (RLBP) limiters in the hybrid LB method, together with the associated macroscopic BP constraints. Numerical experiments examine the convergence order, interface capturing performance, and discontinuity resolution capability of the proposed BP hybrid LB method. The results indicate that it effectively suppresses out-of-bounds behavior in the second-order LB method and reduces numerical dissipation in the first-order LB method, while maintaining the prescribed bounds and discrete mass conservation.

papers.title: XMimic and XSoma: Learning Humanoid Motion Tracking and Locomotion in Under a Minute
papers.abstract: We present XMimic and XSoma, which learn humanoid motion tracking and locomotion on rough terrain in under a minute of training. Both follow SuperMimic, which learns a world model of the robot and optimizes the policy with analytic gradients through short rollouts imagined in this model. Existing implementations of this method do not make use of larger GPUs, as every training iteration is a long chain of small GPU operations that run one after another. XMimic and XSoma therefore shorten this chain and run the steps of every iteration at the same time on up to four GPUs. We compile the complete training loop with JAX, including the MuJoCo Warp simulator. For locomotion, XSoma leaves only the dynamics of the robot to the world model and computes everything else exactly, including the terrain height under the feet. It learns with a horizon of one second and without a critic. On four H100 GPUs, XMimic learns to track all 40 LAFAN1 clips with the Unitree G1 in 0.86 minutes, 3.7 times faster than BlinkMimic on one GPU. XSoma reaches the tracking target that Holosoma's tests set for FastSAC in 0.77 minutes, 12.3 times faster than FastSAC on one GPU, while needing only an eighth of its environment steps.

papers.title: Generative AI-Driven Parametric Design Optimization Framework for Vehicle Closure Systems
papers.abstract: This study presents a generative AI-driven parametric design optimization framework integrating performance-oriented generation with editable computer-aided design (CAD) and downstream computer-aided engineering (CAE) analysis for industrial vehicle closure systems. The framework is demonstrated on an automotive tailgate assembly with complex geometry, coupled components, and competing performance and feasibility requirements. A production-oriented CATIA model is restructured into a reference-based parametric template with a 13-dimensional design representation. An automated CAD/CAE workflow generates parametric models, performs structural analysis, and constructs a database of mass, maximum displacement, and maximum von Mises stress. Gaussian process regression surrogates predict performance, while diffusion and flow matching models generate design candidates. The design problem minimizes mass and maximum displacement, with stress assessed as an engineering feasibility constraint. Performance-guided generation using surrogate guidance and performance-aware training using a performance-aware loss incorporate engineering objectives, with sensitivity to guidance scale and loss weight evaluated. Generative search is compared with NSGA-II under matched evaluation budgets using a common surrogate model. Selected Pareto-region candidates are reconstructed in CATIA and re-evaluated through native CAE; all verified candidates are successfully regenerated and analyzed. Relative to the baseline, the knee-point design reduces mass by 7.1% and maximum displacement by 29.4%, while extreme verified solutions achieve maximum reductions of 10.3% and 37.3%, respectively. The results demonstrate performance-oriented multi-objective design exploration compatible with editable industrial CAD and native engineering verification.

papers.title: On Covariance Steering with Nonlinear Measurements
papers.abstract: This paper examines two ways nonlinear measurements complicate the statistical predictions during covariance steering. The covariance steering problem optimizes a control policy across a distribution of possible trajectories rather than a single specific trajectory. This approach has attracted growing interest as a way to account for uncertainty in aerospace applications such as trajectory optimization, stationkeeping, and landing. In many of these applications, covariance steering can account for measurement uncertainty through output feedback. Because standard formulations assume linear dynamics and measurements, applications with nonlinear measurements typically use an extended Kalman filter to estimate the state. This paper shows that techniques used to improve filter convergence, such as measurement underweighting, can reduce the accuracy of conventional covariance steering predictions by violating a key assumption. This is addressed with a new convex formulation that relaxes the assumption. This paper also demonstrates that adjusting the control policy during execution can improve agreement between predicted and actual state statistics. A numerical example of angles-only spacecraft rendezvous illustrates the benefits of the proposed method, and discussions are made regarding the implications of this generalized covariance steering formulation.

papers.title: Synergistic delivery of FSTL1 and CHIR99021 in 3D bioprinted patches promotes adult mammalian heart repair
papers.abstract: Recent advances in tissue engineering have positioned cardiac patch devices as a promising strategy to restore heart function and structure following myocardial infarction (MI). However, many existing patches are limited by the absence of vascular networks and insufficient biomolecular signals to effectively promote cardiomyocyte (CM) regeneration. In this study, we address these limitations by incorporating follistatin-like 1 (FSTL1) and CHIR99021 (CHIR) into a 3D bioprinted vascularized cardiac patch. The pro-proliferative effects of FSTL1 and CHIR on human induced pluripotent stem cell (hiPSC)-derived CMs were validated in vitro using 2D cultures, 3D hydrogel casts, and 3D bioprinted constructs. The synergistic impact of FSTL1 and CHIR was further evaluated in a rat model of acute MI. Treatment with the CHIR+FSTL1-loaded cardiac patch led to significant improvement in cardiac function and reduced fibrosis. Enhanced angiogenesis and increased CM proliferation were also observed following patch treatment. By integrating 3D bioprinting with targeted regenerative cues, this engineered cardiac patch presents strong therapeutic potential for myocardial repair.

papers.title: A North American experience with the “French Paradox” technique in total hip arthroplasty: up to 5-year follow-up
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Background: Cement use in total hip arthroplasty (THA) is a topic of ongoing research and debate. The French Paradox cement technique, first described in European arthroplasty literature, achieves a thin (<2 mm) cement mantle by preparing the femoral canal only slightly larger than the femoral implant. The technique was coined the “French Paradox” because a French-designed stem showed excellent long-term outcomes despite previous evidence that thin cement mantles can be prone to failure. Purpose: The purpose of this study was to describe a North American experience with femoral stems implanted using the French Paradox cement technique. Study Design/Methods: This was a retrospective study of 125 patients who underwent primary, unilateral THA using the French Paradox cement technique between 2020 and 2023 at 3 academic health systems and had minimum 2-year follow-up. Demographic, implant-related, perioperative, radiographic, and complication variables, as well as patient-reported outcome measures and postoperative variables, were collected at baseline and all available postoperative follow-ups. Chi-square, t test, and ANOVA were used to assess statistical significance, with a significance level of 0.05. Level of Evidence: IV. Results: Of the 125 patients, 84% were women, 86% were White, and 5% were current smokers. The mean age of the cohort was 73 years, the mean Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI) was 3.6%, and 96% of patients had an ASA score of either II or III. There was 1 readmission (0.8%) within 90 days of surgery, which was due to sepsis of gastrointestinal origin. Two patients (1.6%) underwent revision at a mean time of 14 months, 1 for acute PJI and 1 for acetabular component loosening. There were no femoral stem complications, including no instances of loosening, periprosthetic fracture, or stem subsidence. Patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) showed consistent and meaningful improvements in HOOS, JR and Forgotten Joint Score (FJS). Conclusion: The French Paradox cement technique demonstrated exceptional outcomes up to 5 years with no instances of femoral complications (loosening, subsidence, periprosthetic fracture, or stem failure). In appropriately selected patients and with compatible femoral stem designs, the French Paradox cement technique represents an effective cemented femoral fixation strategy with excellent early to mid-term survivorship.

papers.title: Mapping of in-plane biaxial fatigue crack propagation under different loading conditions using finite-element simulations and neural-network surrogate modelling
papers.abstract: Purpose Under biaxial loading conditions, fatigue crack propagation can be very hard to predict, due to different possible propagation modes and the high number of parameters to consider. If mixed mode or out-of-phase conditions are present, crack deflection leads to many possible propagation paths and different failure locations. Therefore, predicting crack behaviour and fatigue life becomes essential if safer part design is to be achieved. This article aims to map crack propagation under different biaxial loading conditions, providing a database of paths and stress intensity factors that can be used as a reference for future part design. Design/methodology/approach To achieve this goal, an idealized reference model was created, where specimen-specific effects on crack propagation can be neglected. When subjected to different stress ratios, biaxial ratios and load phase-shifts, crack propagation was simulated using a previously developed finite element method algorithm. Findings Using randomized loading parameters, a large database was built considering two possible propagation modes. In the end, a machine learning model was used to interpolate the database, providing the full map of possible crack paths, displaying an accurate correlation against the finite element simulations. Originality/value The developed quasi-analytical model provides, for the first time, an extensive map for crack paths and crack driving forces under different biaxial conditions, while the developed machine learning solutions enable the full interpolation of the calculated map. These results enhance fatigue design and unlock optimal specimen development. Highlights:

papers.title: A finite anisotropic thermo-elasto-plastic approach to specimens produced by additive manufacturing
papers.abstract: Purpose The contribution at hand aims at the formulation of a realistic numerical model for solids that are produced by the selective laser melting (SLM) process, which belongs to the powder-bed additive manufacturing (AM) technologies. SLM might induce anisotropy into the solids, depending on process parameters, such as scanning direction and laser power. Furthermore, temperature dependency and intrinsic plastic material characteristics are induced into these solids, since the final part is constitutively close to the processed powder, e.g. AlSi10Mg. Design/methodology/approach A phenomenological constitutive modeling approach at finite anisotropic thermo-elasto-plasticity is introduced. The modeling approach is based on the multiplicative split of the deformation gradient. The evolution equations for the plastic deformation gradient and the hardening strain are introduced in a thermodynamically consistent manner. The approach considers the plastic incompressibility condition and the principle of maximum dissipation. An anisotropic Helmholtz energy is given, considering volumetric thermal deformations. An anisotropic representation of the thermal conductivity behavior is formulated. The set of constitutive equations is consistently linearized and incorporated into a Newton-type solver. Findings A realistic computational modeling to final parts and products of SLM technologies is achieved, based on an anisotropic fully coupled thermo-elasto-plastic material description at finite deformations. The physical applicability of the formulation is validated by different numerical examples, which consider final AlSi10Mg parts. Additionally, the numerical stability and robustness of the proposed modeling is investigated. Originality/value The contribution at hand provides the means to numerically predict structural capabilities for anisotropic thermo-elasto-plastic solids, for example, made from SLM processes.

papers.title: Machine learning algorithms for the prediction of pile impedance in nonhomogeneous soils
papers.abstract: The following data driven and physics informed machine learning models are used in predicting the impedance of pile foundations subject to vertical and lateral dynamic loads: Gaussian Processes, Neural Networks, Decision Trees, and Gradient Boosted Trees. The models were trained on finite element analyses data and predicted the impedance of piles reliably when the input was similar to training data. When predicting impedance for data not used in training, the Gaussian Process and Neural Networks models performed better. Neural Networks was the best performer overall and was selected for further applications. The application of Neural Networks in predicting pile responses against sinusoidal and earthquake loading was examined and compared against different methods. Trained machine learning algorithms can reliably predict the impedance of piles, which would help reduce the time and computational power needed for analyses of piles subjected to dynamic loads and can reduce the number of iterations for finite element analyses.

papers.title: Osteointegration as a biological and mechanical process
papers.abstract: Osseointegration of titanium implants is a complex process determined by the interaction of biological, mechanical, and technological factors. The development of patient-specific implants manufactured using additive technologies provides new opportunities for optimizing bone–implant interactions; however, it also introduces additional requirements for structural design, manufacturing quality, and mechanical reliability. This review summarizes current evidence regarding the biological and mechanical aspects of titanium implant osseointegration, with particular emphasis on porous architectures, manufacturing technologies, and methods for evaluating implant performance. The differences between primary mechanical stability and subsequent biological fixation are discussed, together with the influence of implant micromotion, pore size, interconnectivity, and structural geometry on bone ingrowth. Particular attention is given to laser powder bed fusion, post-processing procedures, manufacturing-induced defects, and fatigue resistance of Ti6Al4V implants. The mechanical and biological characteristics of lattice structures, including gyroid and diamond architectures, are also considered. The available evidence indicates that favorable bone ingrowth does not necessarily ensure adequate mechanical fixation, while improvements in surface properties alone cannot guarantee long-term implant durability. Therefore, reliable evaluation of patient-specific titanium implants requires an integrated approach combining quantitative assessment of bone–implant contact, newly formed bone volume, structural characteristics, and mechanical performance. Further standardization of manufacturing parameters and experimental evaluation methods is essential for improving the reproducibility and clinical applicability of porous titanium implants.

papers.title: Tuning Inter- and Intraparticle Crosslinking and Packing Density Governs the 3D Bioprintability and Biological Performance
papers.abstract: Abstract Granular hydrogels are an emerging class of microporous biomaterials assembled from annealable microparticles that enhance cell survival, function, infiltration, and cell migration through their interconnected cell-scale void spaces. Here, we aimed to understand how balancing inter- and intraparticle interactions, alongside microparticle packing density, influences the printability and cellular responses of granular hydrogels. Mechanically fragmented microparticles, made of tyramine-modified alginate (TAlg) and gelatin (TGel), underwent primary enzymatic gelation and secondary photocrosslinking for construct stabilization. Balancing this two-scale chemical trade-off yielded a compressive modulus of 12.9–24.7 kPa, while rapid photoinitiator clearance (>90% within 1 h) ensured high cytocompatibility. Incorporating 10–40 vol % interstitial matrix tuned total porosity from ∼7 to 18%, with medium-packed inks (20 vol % matrix) achieving high fidelity for three-dimensional (3D) bioprinting without sacrificing void connectivity. The resulting interconnected network accelerated cell infiltration to a depth of 450 μm within 3 days (∼3-fold higher than bulk hydrogels) and enabled ex vivo tissue adhesion (7.1 kPa shear strength). 3D-bioprinted granular constructs supported dense interconnected 3D cellular network formation over 7 days. This scalable strategy to deconstruct di-tyramine-mediated bulk hydrogels provides a versatile toolbox for advanced biofabrication and complex tissue engineering.

papers.title: Ceramic component fracture following trauma in a bilateral total hip arthroplasty
papers.abstract: Background Ceramic-on-ceramic total hip arthroplasty has demonstrated excellent wear characteristics and long-term survivorship. Nevertheless, ceramic component fracture remains a rare but potentially devastating complication. Traumatic events may contribute to failure even in previously well-functioning implants. Case Presentation We report the case of a 66-year-old male who underwent a bilateral ceramic-on-ceramic total hip arthroplasty. The postoperative course was uneventful, and the patient remained asymptomatic with satisfactory function. Three years after the surgery, he sustained an accidental fall. Subsequently, he reported an audible noise originating from the left hip, followed by progressive pain and severe functional limitation. Radiographic and computed tomography (CT) scan evaluation suggested a fracture of the ceramic bearing. Revision surgery was performed, during which the ceramic head and acetabular insert were exchanged. The postoperative course was favourable. Conclusion Although uncommon, ceramic component fracture should be suspected in patients presenting with hip noise, pain, and functional deterioration, particularly following trauma. Early diagnosis and prompt revision are essential to prevent further joint damage and optimize clinical outcomes.

papers.title: A volumetric additive manufacturing machine learning and video-correction method for engineering gelatin methacryloyl and poly(ethylene glycol) diacrylate hydrogel spheres and assembloids
papers.abstract: Abstract Volumetric additive manufacturing (VAM) has emerged as a powerful biofabrication platform capable of rapidly generating complex, freeform, cell-laden constructs. These advantages have positioned VAM as a promising technology for tissue engineering. However, widespread adoption for bottom-up tissue engineering and bioassembly applications remains limited by optical dose heterogeneities, material-dependent polymerization behavior, and post-fabrication swelling or shrinkage, all of which reduce dimensional accuracy and reproducibility. Here, we present two complementary, open-source correction strategies to improve print fidelity in VAM: (i) an attention-based machine learning (ML) framework and (ii) a real-time video-guided correction workflow. The ML framework employs a dimensionally reduced representation of volumetric print data encoded as stacked 2D arrays with print metadata, enabling efficient model training without specialized computing hardware. Using random shape arrays printed in gelatin methacryloyl (GelMA) and poly(ethylene glycol) diacrylate (PEGDA), we trained a metadata-informed attention U-Net to generate corrected print arrays that compensate for material-specific printing errors. ML correction improved fine-feature fidelity in GelMA constructs, enhancing corner sharpness and volume recapitulation. However, the ML approach did not provide benefits for PEGDA formulations. In parallel, we developed a video-based correction workflow that directly compensates for z-axis polymerization heterogeneities without requiring material-specific model training. A universal video correction model generated from a PEGDA phantom was successfully applied to optically transparent GelMA bioinks, enabling accurate fabrication without recalibration. Using this approach, hundreds of highly uniform hydrogel spheroids were fabricated in less than 30 s and integrated into melt electrowritten (MEW) scaffolds for bioassembly applications. Cell-laden U87 GelMA spheroids maintained high viability, exhibited extensive F-actin organization and collagen VI deposition, and initiated early spheroid fusion following both video corrected VAM and bioassembly processes. Collectively, these results establish both ML- and video-corrected VAM as facile workflows for reproducible spheroid fabrication for bottom-up biofabrication of complex tissues across a broad range of biomaterials.

papers.title: 4D bioprinting materials: Revolutionizing biomedical applications using smart and stimuli-responsive systems
papers.abstract: 4D bioprinting, an emerging additive manufacturing technology, is used for creating biomedical constructs with programmed changes in shape, properties, or function over time. Unlike conventional 3D printing techniques producing static structures, 4D bioprinting integrates stimuli-responsive biomaterials to generate dynamic and adaptive constructs. This functionality is achieved by utilizing stimuli-responsive hydrogels, shape-memory polymers (SMPs), conductive polymers, magnetic-responsive systems, and natural polymer-based bioinks. Common responsive materials include poly(N-isopropylacrylamide), polyethylene glycol, polypyrrole, and polyaniline, while SMPs are PLA, PGDA, and polyurethanes; natural ones like polymer-acrylate blends of gelatin, hyaluronan, and alginate enable transformations. These materials respond to stimuli like temperature, light, pH, magnetic/electrical signals, and changes in biological environment and help in advancing drug delivery, tissue engineering, and regenerative medicine. These materials with adaptive and spatially controlled properties have eventually transformed overall patient-specific treatments. This review furnishes account on these aforementioned 4D bioprinting systems including their actuation mechanisms, printability, biocompatibility, functional performance, and translational potential. Printing resolution, manufacturing reproducibility, control over transition kinetics, interfacial mechanics, long-term biosafety, and regulatory requirements are barriers limiting their clinical translation. Hence, future progression is highly dependent upon development of highly biocompatible multi-responsive materials with improved spatiotemporal control of actuation, standardized manufacturing and characterization strategies, and robust validation.

papers.title: Primary Hyperparathyroidism May Not Be Associated With Adverse Clinical and Functional Outcomes After Total Hip Arthroplasty
papers.abstract: Introduction Primary hyperparathyroidism (PHPT) can result in reduced bone mineral density and increased fracture risk. Total hip arthroplasty (THA) is commonly performed for end-stage osteoarthritis, but the metabolic effects of PHPT on perioperative outcomes are unclear. We evaluated PHPT's association with clinical and functional outcomes following THA. Materials and methods This was a single-center retrospective study of patients who underwent primary THA from January 2016 to December 2024. Patients who underwent biochemical evaluation for parathyroid disease (PHPT versus controls) were included. All patients completed the Hip Disability and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score for Joint Replacement (HOOS-JR), a validated instrument assessing THA-related hip function, at baseline and one year after THA. Postoperative improvements in HOOS-JR scores were compared between groups. Multivariable regression was used to identify factors predicting failure in postoperative improvement. Results Of 13,487 patients who underwent THA, 519 (3.8%) underwent biochemical evaluation: 155 with PHPT (15.5% classic, 69.7% normocalcemic, 14.8% normohormonal) and 364 controls. The PHPT cohort had slightly lower baseline [39.9 (IQR: 29.0-47.5) versus 43.3 (IQR: 32.7-53.0), P = 0.018] and 1-y [76.8 (IQR: 64.7-92.3) versus 85.4 (IQR: 70.4-100), P = 0.031] HOOS-JR scores compared to controls. Both groups observed significant improvement (95% versus 92%, P = 0.702), while reported rates of satisfaction tended to be worse with PHPT (49% versus 62%, P = 0.053), one year after surgery. PHPT was not independently associated with poorer patient-reported outcomes postoperatively (OR: 0.71, 95% CI: 0.22-2.28, P = 0.568). Conclusions PHPT was not an independent predictor of decreased clinical or functional outcomes following THA. These findings suggest that patients diagnosed with PHPT may safely pursue THA and expect meaningful improvement in symptoms.

papers.title: Comparative Evaluation of Immediate vs. Delayed Loading Protocols for Dental Implants in the Esthetic Zone: A Structured Narrative Review
papers.abstract: The timing of loading is a central decision in implant therapy in the esthetic zone, where patients value shorter treatment but the peri-implant tissues leave little room for error. Methods. Targeted search of international consensus reports, systematic reviews and meta-analyses and randomized trials up to September 2026 were used to identify methods. No new meta-analysis conducted, published estimates were re-plotted. Results. No significant difference between immediate and conventional loading in terms of 1-year survival (risk ratio 0.99; 95% CI 0.95–1.02), marginal bone loss or papilla and midfacial mucosa level was found in pooled randomized trials, though the trials were small and the risk of bias was unclear. The weighted mean survival of immediate placement with immediate loading (Type 1A) exceeded 97.7% (95% CI 96.9–98.4) across 68 studies, provided that only very few patients and very few centers were included. Immediate placement was associated with a higher deviation from esthetic outcome and to midfacial recession in >26% of cases in a median of 1 mm. There was no difference between the immediate provisionalization and conventional loading in terms of patient-reported outcomes. Conclusions. Immediate loading is a viable option in select, single-tooth sites with sufficient primary stability, intact facial bone wall, a thick soft-tissue phenotype and a provisional restoration that is not placed in occlusion. When these conditions are not present delayed loading, or early placement, is still safer. While plenty of short-term trials are being conducted, there is still a need for well-designed long-term clinical trials with standardized esthetic endpoints.

papers.title: XPINN-based parametric modeling method for solving magnetic fields with moving boundaries
papers.abstract: Purpose Moving-boundary magnetic field analysis in multi-material electromagnetic devices is computationally expensive because boundary motion requires finite element (FE) mesh updates, while material nonlinearity requires iterative solutions. An extended physics-informed neural network (XPINN)-based parametric framework was developed for efficient and accurate magnetic field prediction for such devices. Design/methodology/approach The computational domain was divided into material- and topology-based subdomains, with local fields represented by dedicated subnetworks coupled through interface continuity conditions. This architecture was designed to handle discontinuities in material properties and the complex magnetic-field distributions near the interfaces. To avoid repeated sampling due to moving boundaries, a geometry-state-driven dynamic sampling strategy was proposed to reassign sampling points between subdomains and update moving-interface samples and constraints according to the mover position, enabling parametric prediction across different displacements. Findings The predicted magnetic vector potential and magnetic flux density of an electrodynamic shaker agreed well with the high-fidelity FE results, with maximum relative errors of 0.77% and 0.78%, respectively. The framework achieved speedups of 5.14–21.95 times for multi-case predictions. Compared with a standard physics-informed neural network, it reduced the maximum point-wise absolute errors in vector potential and flux density by 96.72% and 99.07%, respectively, while reducing the flux density error by 15.71% relative to a resampled XPINN. Originality/value The framework combined XPINN with the proposed geometry-state-driven sampling strategy, providing a potentially generalizable approach for efficient and accurate electromagnetic-field prediction in systems with heterogeneous media and moving boundaries.

papers.title: Hybrid MPC for dual three-phase PMSMs under open-phase and short-circuit faults
papers.abstract: This paper presents a unified, constraint-preserving polynomial hybrid model predictive control (MPC) strategy for dual three-phase permanent magnet synchronous motors (DT-PMSMs) under open-phase faults (OPFs) and short-circuit faults (SCFs). For OPFs, a cubic polynomial mixing coefficient approximates the full-range minimum-loss (FRML) optimal solution, guaranteeing rated current limits. For SCFs, a two-stage Lagrange-based compensation cancels the short-circuit magnetomotive force (MMF) and applies the open-phase hybrid strategy. Both fault modes are integrated into a finite control set MPC (FCS-MPC) framework with 12 virtual voltage vectors (VVs) that produce zero harmonic voltage. Experimental validation on a DT-PMSM prototype shows that under healthy conditions the currents are sinusoidal and balanced. Under an uncompensated OPF, the currents become severely distorted and unbalanced (peak > 1.75 p.u.). The proposed OPF controller restores sinusoidal balanced currents within the rated limit (1 p.u.) and suppresses harmonic currents, as seen from the z 1 z 2 trajectories collapsing to a small cluster near the origin. Under an SCF, the controller maintains sinusoidal αβ currents matching the torque reference (0.5 p.u.) while keeping the non-sinusoidal phase currents within the rated limit. Dynamic tests show that under OPF, a load torque step of 6 Nm causes a speed drop of < 6% with recovery in 150 ms and a torque overshoot of 7%; a speed step from 500 to 700 r/min has a rise time of 70 ms with negligible overshoot. The algorithm runs in 80 µs on a TMS320F28335 DSP, confirming real-time feasibility.

papers.title: Computationally Efficient Topology Optimization of Lightweight Structures: An Integrated Perspective on Adaptive Mesh Refinement, Hybrid Search, and Machine Learning
papers.abstract: Topology optimization (TO) supported by finite element analysis (FEA) offers a systematic means of distributing material within a prescribed design domain to achieve structural performance objectives under material and loading constraints. However, computational expense, mesh sensitivity, convergence difficulties, and the growing complexity of design requirements can limit its use in large-scale engineering problems. This paper develops a conceptual synthesis of three complementary directions discussed in the source thesis: adaptive mesh refinement (AMR), hybrid optimization algorithms, and machine-learning-assisted design exploration. It explains how AMR can concentrate finite element resolution in regions where the solution or structural response changes rapidly; how hybrid search strategies may combine complementary exploration and exploitation behaviours; and how machine learning may support surrogate modelling, design-space screening, and parameter selection. A staged computational framework is proposed in which a baseline FEA model is followed by topology optimization, error-informed mesh adaptation, optional hybrid search, and independent verification of the final design. The paper does not report new numerical experiments or claim measured performance improvements. Instead, it identifies the data, benchmark problems, validation procedures, and reproducibility information required to test the proposed framework. The synthesis provides a research agenda for developing computationally efficient and verifiable lightweight structural designs.

papers.title: Architected metamaterials fabricated by 3D printing for enhanced compression strength and energy dissipation
papers.abstract: This study investigates the effect of arc count, the number of Schwarz Primitive (P) unit cells distributed around the circumference, on the mechanical response and energy absorption of hollow cylindrical TPMS structures. Five configurations (3, 5, 7, 9, and 11 arcs) were analyzed by finite element analysis, and the Arc 3 configuration was validated experimentally. Increasing the arc count from 3–11 raised the relative density from 0.196 to 0.268, the stiffness by 91.6%, and the effective modulus by 92.5%. The normalized modulus reached 54% to 75% of the axial upper bound, indicating predominantly axial load carrying with an efficiency that rose with arc count, and an empirical power law gave an exponent of 2.12 (R 2 = 0.993). All configurations entered the hardening region at 3.7–3.8% strain and showed no softening up to 13.25% strain. Specific energy absorption (SEA) rose by approximately 97.9% and toughness from 166 to 300 J/m 3 , with diminishing gains at higher arc counts. The force-response indicators, however, were non-monotonic: Arc 7 exhibited the highest behavior factor (1.16) and the lowest crush force efficiency (0.86), whereas Arc 3 showed the lowest behavior factor (1.07) and the highest crush force efficiency (0.93). The experimental response agreed with the simulation within 1% in force and stress at 5 mm and within 3.5% and 8.5% in SEA and toughness, respectively. Arc count is therefore an effective design variable for tailoring the stiffness and energy absorption of Schwarz-P cylinders, although gains in energy absorption and crushing-force uniformity do not necessarily occur together.

papers.title: Pyvale: A Fast, Scalable, Open-Source 2D Digital Image Correlation (DIC) Engine Capable of Handling Gigapixel Images
papers.abstract: Abstract Background Digital Image Correlation (DIC) is a widely used full‑field measurement technique, but both open‑source and commercial packages often have limitations such as operating‑system restrictions, lack of support for deployment on computing clusters, and poor scalability to gigapixel‑scale images common in Scanning Electron Microscopy DIC (SEM-DIC). Objective Pyvale is an open‑source software package designed for sensor simulation, uncertainty quantification, placement optimization, and calibration/validation. A key component of this is the development of a dedicated 2D DIC module intended for standalone use and integration within broader workflows. Methods Pyvale provides a user‑friendly Python interface with performant compiled routines underneath. At its core is a multithreaded, reliability‑guided DIC algorithm. Its open‑source MIT license enables wide deployment, including on computing clusters and in automated pipelines. Results Benchmarking with the publicly available 2D DIC challenge 2.0 dataset shows that Pyvale achieves metrological performance comparable to existing commercial and open-source DIC codes. It can correlate gigapixel‑scale image pairs in under 5 minutes on high-specification desktop workstations, with memory peaking at approximately 50 GB. Conclusions Pyvale ’s strong metrological foundation, coupled with its scalability for SEM‑DIC, positions it as a platform for sustained, community‑driven development. Its design and licensing provide a foundation for future improvements in open‑source DIC and integration into experimental design and validation workflows.

papers.title: Surrogate-Based Bayesian Calibration Methods for Chaotic Systems: A Comparison of Traditional and Nontraditional Approaches
papers.abstract: Abstract. Parameter calibration is essential for reducing uncertainty and improving predictive fidelity in physics-based models, yet it is often limited by the high computational cost of model evaluations. Bayesian calibration methods provide a principled framework for combining prior information with data while rigorously quantifying uncertainty. In this work, we compare four emulator-based Bayesian calibration strategies—Calibrate–Emulate–Sample (CES), History Matching (HM), Bayesian Optimal Experimental Design (BOED), and a goal-oriented extension of BOED (GBOED)—using the Lorenz ’96 multiscale system and a two-layer quasi-geostrophic (QG) model as test cases. The proposed GBOED formulation explicitly targets information gain with respect to the calibration posterior, aligning design decisions with downstream inference. We assess methods using accuracy and uncertainty quantification metrics, convergence behavior under increasing computational budgets, and practical considerations such as implementation complexity and robustness. For the Lorenz ’96 system, CES, HM, and GBOED all yield strong calibration performance, even with limited numbers of model evaluations, while standard BOED generally underperforms in this setting. Differences among the strongest methods are modest, particularly as computational budgets increase. For the QG system, all methods produce reasonable posterior estimates, and convergence behavior is more consistent, reflecting smoother parameter–statistic relationships and improved identifiability. Overall, our results indicate that multiple emulator-based calibration strategies can perform comparably well when applied appropriately, with method selection often guided more by computational and practical considerations than by accuracy alone. These findings highlight both the limitations of standard BOED for calibration and the promise of goal-oriented and iterative approaches for efficient Bayesian inference in complex dynamical systems.
